name: Hardmaxxing

lead: Hardmaxxing is the invasive end of looksmaxxing: surgery, injectables, drugs and peptides, as opposed to skincare, grooming and fitness (softmaxxing). The payoff is a structural change to the face or body, such as jaw, nose or skin, that softer methods do not reach.

Surgical methods change bone or soft-tissue shape directly; injectables and drugs act on muscle, skin, hormones or growth pathways. The label spans established procedures like rhinoplasty and jaw surgery as well as botulinum toxin, hair transplants and limb-lengthening, plus fringe practices such as bonesmashing. Established procedures produce visible results, while DIY and fringe variants are poorly studied.

paras: Forum users typically build personalised plans combining several methods, starting with consultations for surgical or medical options and then layering softmaxxing around them. Recovery and visible results vary by procedure, from days for injectables to months for surgery.

Surgeons warn of complications, especially with unsupervised or overseas procedures, and of fractures and asymmetry from bonesmashing. Steroids carry hormonal and cardiovascular effects. A 2026 study of social media discourse examined self-injection and DIY procedures among 'dangerous' trends, and commentators link looksmaxxing with body dysmorphia.

studies.title: Dangerous trends on social media related to facial esthetics: Analysis of looksmaxxing and its softmaxxing and hardmaxxing practices.
studies.source: Journal of stomatology, oral and maxillofacial surgery

chain: Structural change to face or body
angle.text: Hardmaxxing is looksmaxxing slang for invasive methods such as surgery, fillers and off-label drugs, used for changes to the jaw, nose or skin that softer methods do not reach. Established procedures change the structure directly and produce visible results; DIY and fringe variants are poorly studied.

lead: Hardmaxxing is looksmaxxing slang for invasive or medically intensive ways of changing appearance, as opposed to 'softmaxxing', which covers non-invasive practices such as skincare, grooming, clothing and fitness. People who hardmaxx aim to change the structures that soft methods cannot reach: the shape of the nose, jaw, chin, eye area or hairline, or the body's hormonal and muscular profile. [1][2]

The term covers cosmetic and maxillofacial surgery such as rhinoplasty and jaw surgery, injectables such as botulinum toxin and fillers, and the use of off-label drugs and peptides. Wikipedia and Grokipedia also list limb-lengthening, hair transplants and steroid use among practices placed under the label, and describe bonesmashing, striking the face, as an extreme and widely criticised fringe idea. [1][3]

Surgeons and other clinicians have commented publicly on the trend. A plastic surgeon at UT Southwestern describes hardmaxxing as the riskier end of looksmaxxing, and a 2026 cross-sectional study of social media discourse about 'dangerous' facial aesthetic trends examined looksmaxxing and its softmaxxing and hardmaxxing practices, including DIY procedures, self-injection and bonesmashing. [4][5]
infobox: Rhinoplasty, jaw surgery, botulinum toxin, genioplasty, hair transplant, off-label drugs and peptides [1][3]
From incel-linked forums in the 2010s to TikTok, YouTube and livestreams in the 2020s [1][3][4]
Surgery and prescription drugs are regulated medical products or procedures; research peptides are generally not approved for these uses [1]
Surgical complications, DIY filler injuries, hormonal effects, body dysmorphia [3][9][5]

paras: Within looksmaxxing, practices are commonly sorted into soft and hard. Wikipedia describes softmaxxing as non-invasive (skincare, grooming, clothing, fitness, and also contested practices like mewing) and hardmaxxing as more extreme measures such as off-label substances, extreme dieting, skin whitening and cosmetic surgery. [1] Dr. Christine Stiles of UT Southwestern, writing in 2026, likewise defines hardmaxxing as the riskier end of looksmaxxing, including anabolic steroid use, cosmetic surgery and self-harm practices such as bone smashing, and softmaxxing as diet, exercise, skincare and supplements. [5]

Grokipedia lists surgical examples as jaw implants, genioplasty, rhinoplasty, hair transplants and limb or clavicle lengthening, as well as steroid use and travel abroad for cheaper procedures. It says many participants travel to Turkey for cheaper procedures and lists infections, botched results, nerve damage, facial asymmetry and fractures among reported complications. [3]

Users on looksmax.org draw up personal hardmaxxing plans that list facial procedures such as maxillary surgeries, rhinoplasty and lip surgery alongside injectables and peptides, often noting that choices differ by individual. One poster's plan, for example, pairs micro-botulinum toxin for eye and mouth asymmetry with a maxillary advancement and a rhinoplasty. [2][6][7]

Facial procedures named in forum plans and in clinician commentary include bimaxillary osteotomy (repositioning of the upper and lower jaws), LeFort 1 maxillary advancement, genioplasty and chin implants, jaw implants, rhinoplasty and blepharoplasty. Dr. Stiles notes that major facial bone surgeries are generally reserved for congenital deformities or injuries from accidents, rather than elective appearance changes. [2][3][5]

Body-based surgeries, notably limb and clavicle lengthening, also appear under the label. Grokipedia cites reported risks including infection, nerve damage and long recovery, and the 2025 Sociology of Health & Illness study of a looksmaxxing forum records leg-lengthening surgery among the drastic changes the community encourages. [3][8]
Hair transplants are listed as another hardmaxxing option aimed at the hairline and frame of the face. [3]

Non-surgical hardmaxxing includes botulinum toxin, dermal fillers, off-label anabolic steroids, human growth hormone, aromatase inhibitors and peptides. Wikipedia notes that the peptide GHK-Cu is widely used in topical cosmetics, while injectable versions bought through unregulated channels have drawn an FDA warning about the lack of human testing. [1]

Beverly Hills plastic surgeon Dr. Joseph Hadid and cosmetic surgeon Dr. Anthony Youn, quoted by the Daily Dot in 2026, describe participants using black-market injectable fillers and unregulated supplements, sometimes administered to themselves or others without medical training. [9]

Bonesmashing, striking one's own face with a hard object in the belief that the resulting changes add definition, is usually described as the extreme edge of the category. Wikipedia calls it an inside joke that is rarely carried out; clinicians describe it as dangerous. [1][9]

A 2026 cross-sectional study counted 2,518 mentions of 'bonesmashing' over 12 months, an estimated reach of 32 million and a rise of about 5,000 percent in related search interest compared with the prior year. [4]

Wikipedia reports that looksmaxxing began on incel-associated message boards in the 2010s, including PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.net, and moved to TikTok in the early 2020s. The split between 'soft' and 'hard' methods is part of the vocabulary that grew up around those communities and tier lists. [1] Grokipedia adds that hashtags and before-and-after videos on TikTok spread the practice around 2020, and that Reddit, 4chan, Discord and Telegram groups carried it between platforms. [3]

By the mid-2020s, hardmaxxing appeared in mainstream news. Wikipedia lists coverage in the New York Times, The Guardian and GQ in February 2026 on the Kick livestreamer Braden Peters, known as Clavicular, and records a livestreamed overdose in April 2026 involving a drug mixture that Wikipedia says was promoted by another influencer as sustainable. [1] The Daily Dot reported that Clavicular livestreamed a rhinoplasty on 3 June 2026, and quoted Dr. Youn describing him as early in the healing process. [9]

In the 2026 social media study, YouTube accounted for 43.7 percent of the discussion analysed and TikTok for 17.4 percent. Content tagged #bonesmashing was about 98 percent male and #mewing about 74 percent male. [4]

The 2026 study in the Journal of Stomatology, Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery used the Brand24 social-listening tool, Google Trends and Instagram engagement metrics, then a thematic analysis of the 100 most-engaged posts promoting looksmaxxing practices. It found 65 percent neutral, 18 percent negative and 17 percent positive sentiment, and identified four narratives: self-improvement as empowerment, pseudoscientific legitimacy, community belonging and mutual validation, and risk minimisation and normalisation. Its authors conclude that dangerous practices are being normalised through pseudoscientific language and community validation. [4]

The 2025 study in Sociology of Health & Illness analysed 8,072 comments from a looksmaxxing forum with about six million monthly visitors. The authors report that users critique men's bodies from a hegemonic masculine perspective, that the community encourages drastic body changes such as leg-lengthening surgery and mewing, and that users experience 'masculine demoralisation'. They conclude that such communities can harm the health of the men who take part. [8]

Wikipedia reports that surgeons warn of fractures, misalignment and vision damage from bonesmashing, and that a 2025 paper advised physicians to help patients tell safe beauty practices from harmful ones. Commentators have also linked looksmaxxing with body dysmorphia and suicidal ideation. [1]

In a May 2026 Fox News segment, New York dermatologist Dr. Claire Wolinsky called hardmaxxing the more dangerous path, citing steroids, supplements and plastic surgery at a young age, and said breaking bone does not make it thicker or improve the jawline. Family therapist Tom Kersting said influencers often have little real expertise. [10] Dr. Stiles advises checking an adviser's medical credentials, reminds teens that faces soften and change with development, and suggests seeking a realistic assessment from a board-certified plastic surgeon before surgery. [5]

Surgery and prescription drugs are regulated; botulinum toxin, fillers, anabolic steroids and growth hormone require medical supervision or prescription in many countries, while research peptides are generally not approved for these uses. [1]

Reported risks include complications from unsupervised or overseas procedures, fat necrosis and bone injury from bonesmashing, which Dr. Stiles says can lead to a cycle of corrective surgery, and hormonal and cardiovascular effects of steroids. [3][5] Dr. Youn and Dr. Hadid report seeing complications from self-administered fillers. [9]

Wikipedia records that GLP-1 drugs, approved for obesity and type 2 diabetes, are obtained through the grey market by some people without those conditions, and describes a multi-drug mixture that was linked to an April 2026 livestream overdose. [1]

Many forum threads discuss hardmaxxing as a way to approximate favourable bone structure, with questions about how much it can change appearance and what is realistic. Other threads explicitly ask for advice without hardmaxxing, showing that the community treats it as a separate, more serious tier. [6][11]

Grokipedia notes that some looksmaxxing communities have moved away from fatalism toward incremental self-improvement, and that fat loss is often described as the largest non-surgical upgrade. [3] Members who rank methods as 'cope' or 'not cope' often place surgery and body-fat changes in the latter group. [3]

No studies of 'hardmaxxing' as a defined practice were found as clinical trials. The individual procedures grouped under it, such as rhinoplasty and orthognathic surgery, have their own clinical literature, and the 2026 social-media study cited above analyses online discussion rather than clinical outcomes. [4]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, hardmaxxing is discussed as the invasive end of the 'ascension' toolkit, with planning threads, cost questions and debates about how far surgery can mimic good bone structure. [6][7][11]

claims.claim: Surgery and medical procedures can substantially change facial structure.
Peptides and research chemicals add to hardmaxxing results for bones, skin and hair.
Bonesmashing is a form of hardmaxxing.
Travelling abroad (often Turkey) makes hardmaxxing affordable.
Hardmaxxing can approximate good bone structure.
Influencer drug and injectable regimens are safe and sustainable.

timeline.event: Looksmaxxing vocabulary develops on incel-linked forums such as PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.net. [1][3]
Reddit bans r/incels, one of the venues Grokipedia lists among looksmaxxing's early discussion spaces. [3]
Looksmaxxing content spreads on TikTok through before-and-after videos. [1][3]
Business Insider and Vice cover looksmaxxing and hunter eyes; the Daily Dot reports most participants are in their late teens. [1]
Sociology of Health & Illness publishes a qualitative study of a looksmaxxing forum; a paper advises physicians on separating safe from harmful beauty practices. [1][8]

The New York Times, The Guardian and GQ cover Clavicular (February); a social-media study of dangerous facial aesthetic trends appears in the Journal of Stomatology, Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery. [1][4]

A livestreamed overdose (April), a Fox News segment with dermatologist Dr. Claire Wolinsky (May), a livestreamed rhinoplasty (3 June) and a UT Southwestern surgeon's guidance (July) bring hardmaxxing to wider coverage. [1][9][10][5]
